page.title: Balloon-Dropped Flight Test Vehicle
page.tagline: **Dropped from 20,000 ft. Logging every shake.** An instrumented nose cone that measures its own structural vibration as it falls. I worked on the deployment mechanism and data acquisition for the 2,000 ft Phase S1 drop, then built the Teensy 4.1 flight computer that logged the 20,000 ft balloon drop and fired the parachute.

blocks.alt: Video of the Phase S1 scaled cone drone drop near Las Cruces, 3 Dec 2025
blocks.caption: Phase S1: the scaled cone's drone drop near Las Cruces, 3 Dec 2025.

sections.heading: The mission
sections.text: HAWC, the High Altitude Weather Cone, is a research project in NMSU's Environmental Testing of Structures Laboratory with Los Alamos National Laboratory and NMSU's Physical Science Laboratory (PSL). The goal is to drop an instrumented 6061 aluminum nose cone from a balloon at 100,000 ft and record how its internal structure vibrates as it falls through transonic speeds.

sections.heading: Where I came in
sections.html:
Before me: 2022 to 2025

Earlier team members designed and machined the aluminum cone, ran the CFD and thermal qualification, and flew the first drone drops and the first 100,000 ft attempt.

My part: Phases S1 and S2

On the Phase S1 drone drop I worked on part of the deployment mechanism and the data acquisition. For Phase S2, a 20,000 ft balloon drop, I built the flight computer that logged the flight and released the parachute.

figures.caption: Design review with PSL (Physical Science Laboratory) for system validation.

sections.heading: Flight computer
sections.text:
- Teensy 4.1 running embedded C++, logging at 50 Hz.
- Two sources of altitude, GPS and a barometer, plus an IMU and a separate 20 g accelerometer.
- Decides on its own when to deploy, then fires a burn-wire that releases the parachute.
- A status screen for ground checks shows the flight state, GPS fix, both altitudes, every acceleration axis, the reed switch, the countdown and the burn-wire.

figures.alt: Small colour display wired to a Teensy, showing STATE: ARMED, GPS fix and altitude, accelerometer readings, reed switch closed and burn wire on standby
figures.caption: Ground-check screen: armed, burn-wire on standby

figures.alt: Teensy 4.1 on a breadboard wired to a pressure sensor board
figures.caption: Bench build: Teensy 4.1 with the pressure sensor (First model).

sections.heading: What Phase S2 had to prove
sections.text:
Phase S1 showed that the electronics were the weak point. For S2 the team wrote pass/fail criteria for every subsystem, to be checked in the lab before flight. The ones that shaped the flight computer:
- The parachute releases within 2 seconds of the command, 10 times out of 10, including at −30 °C.
- The burn-wire cuts only what it is meant to cut, with no damage to the paracord or canopy.
- Telemetry runs for the whole mission plus a 30-minute margin, and a brownout can't reboot it or lose data.
- Data is recorded continuously, with no gaps or missing timestamps, and the files open afterward.
- GPS puts the recovery team within 10 m of the cone.

figures.alt: Flight profile diagram: balloon ascent to about 20,000 ft, test article release, free fall, parachute release near 1,000 ft, and impact points for the cone and the tow balloon
figures.caption: Phase S2 flight profile from the team's test plan: release near 20,000 ft, parachute at about 1,000 ft.

sections.heading: Test campaign
sections.html:
1. Earlier team
    Aluminum cone, analysis and qualification · from 2022

    CFD of the cone's center of pressure matched NASA wind-tunnel data to within 0.9–4.5% from Mach 0.8 to 1.4. The shell survived a cold soak to −70 °C, and the parachute plate was thickened from 0.25 to 0.375 in after static testing.

  2. Failed
    First 100,000 ft balloon drop

    The parachute did not deploy and telemetry cut out in free fall. The scaled cone and its data were never recovered.

  3. Replan
    Fail fast, in four phases

    The team switched to a 3D-printed scaled cone and a stepped plan with pass/fail criteria at each step: S1 at 2,000 ft, S2 at 20,000 ft, then S3 and S4 at 100,000 ft.

  4. Partial · I joined
    Phase S1 · 2,000 ft drone drop · 3 Dec 2025

    The parachute deployed and the cone was recovered 1,320 ft from release. But the electronics and data acquisition failed, and the ballast didn't lower the center of mass enough for stable flight.

  5. Main phase
    Phase S2 · 20,000 ft AGL balloon drop · 2026

    My flight computer logged GPS, barometric altitude, IMU and a 20 g accelerometer at 50 Hz, and fired the burn-wire parachute release on its own. It worked on the live drop.

  6. Next
    Phases S3 and S4 · 100,000 ft

    Full-altitude drops of the scaled cone, then the aluminum cone with its final data acquisition system.

card.title: Klann walker
card.summary: An eight-legged walking robot driven by linkages and steered from a phone.

image.alt: The 3D-printed Klann walker robot with black legs and white gears

page.title: Klann Linkage Walking Robot
page.tagline: **One crank. Eight legs. A full step.** An eight-legged walker for ME 326 Machine Design. Each leg is a six-link Klann mechanism, so a single rotating crank produces a full walking step. Two servos drive it, and a phone app steers it over Bluetooth.

items.alt: Team members holding the finished walker: white 3D-printed chassis and gears with black linkage legs
items.caption: The finished walker: printed chassis, gear train and linkage legs

items.alt: The project team in a classroom, holding the walker
items.caption: The project team with the finished robot

sections.heading: Why a Klann linkage
sections.text: Our first concept was a hexapod with two-link legs driven by crank-rockers and DC motors. Moving to the Klann linkage gave a longer, flatter stride from the same crank: the foot moves along the ground in a near-straight line, then lifts and swings back, with no servo per joint and no gait code. All the walking comes from link geometry.

sections.heading: Drivetrain and machine elements
sections.text:
- Two continuous-rotation servos, one per side, each driving a 20T pinion into a 50T driven gear (module 1.5) for a 2.5:1 reduction.
- 3/8 in keyed 1045 steel shafts on four ball bearings, each carrying four crank hubs.
- Cranks phased 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° on the left with a 90° offset on the right, so some feet are always on the ground.
- PLA chassis plates (220 × 80 mm) on 35 mm standoffs, with M3 shoulder screws as pivot pins for 32 joints.

sections.heading: Control
sections.text: An Arduino Uno reads one-letter commands (forward, back, pivot left, pivot right, stop) from an HC-05 Bluetooth module, sent by an Android app built in MIT App Inventor. Steering is differential: the sides run at different speeds or opposite directions. Every speed change ramps over 15 steps so the gears and linkages don't take shock loads, and a repeated command is ignored so the robot doesn't stutter.
sections.html:
Phone app
Tap a command

Forward · Both sides drive forward

  1. HC-05 Bluetoothreceives 'F'
  2. handleCommand()case 'F' → L +80, R +80
  3. rampBoth()15 small steps, never a jump
  4. writeMicroseconds()stop pulse +240 / +240 µs
Left servo
+80
Right servo
+80

Pivot left · Sides run opposite: turns in place to the left

  1. HC-05 Bluetoothreceives 'L'
  2. handleCommand()case 'L' → L −65, R +65
  3. rampBoth()15 small steps, never a jump
  4. writeMicroseconds()stop pulse −195 / +195 µs
Left servo
−65
Right servo
+65

Stop · Both servos ramp down to the stop pulse

  1. HC-05 Bluetoothreceives 'S'
  2. handleCommand()case 'S' → L 0, R 0
  3. rampBoth()15 small steps, never a jump
  4. writeMicroseconds()stop pulse 0 / 0 µs
Left servo
0
Right servo
0

Pivot right · Sides run opposite: turns in place to the right

  1. HC-05 Bluetoothreceives 'R'
  2. handleCommand()case 'R' → L +65, R −65
  3. rampBoth()15 small steps, never a jump
  4. writeMicroseconds()stop pulse +195 / −195 µs
Left servo
+65
Right servo
−65

Back · Both sides drive backward, slower than forward

  1. HC-05 Bluetoothreceives 'B'
  2. handleCommand()case 'B' → L −55, R −55
  3. rampBoth()15 small steps, never a jump
  4. writeMicroseconds()stop pulse −165 / −165 µs
Left servo

Right servo
−55

Each speed change ramps over 15 steps (watch the bars) so the gears and linkages don't take shock loads. Sending the same command twice does nothing.

sections.heading: Testing and iteration
sections.text: Our first test drove the walker from the phone over Bluetooth for the first time. After that we ran several more tries focused on making it faster, and we added small grip pads to the feet so the legs get more traction.

card.title: Orbital mechanics
card.summary: Why Mars seems to go backward, proven with 50 years of real NASA data. Plus a live rendezvous planner.

image.alt: Looping plot of Mars's path as seen from Earth

page.kicker: Python · MATLAB · NASA JPL Horizons · AE 424
page.title: Fifty Years of Mars
page.tagline: **Why does Mars sometimes go backward?** 50 years of real NASA data, one clear answer, and Mars's orbit rebuilt from scratch.

blocks.alt: 3D animation built from NASA Horizons data: with Earth fixed at the centre, the Sun circles it and Mars traces a growing pattern of loops
blocks.caption: My 3D animation with Earth held still at the centre. The Sun circles, and Mars traces loops. Every point is real NASA Horizons data.

sections.heading: Why this is cool
sections.html:
The puzzle
Every two years, Mars moonwalks.

It slows down, drifts backward across the sky for about two months, then carries on as if nothing happened.

  1. ~150 ADPtolemy

    Earth at the centre. The loops get explained with circles on circles.

  2. 1543Copernicus

    Puts the Sun at the centre. The loops become a trick of perspective.

  3. 1609Kepler

    Cracks Mars's real orbit: an ellipse. Right inside our 1600–1650 data.

  4. TodayUs

    18,264 days of NASA positions, and code to test it all.

We went further than "it's a perspective effect". We measured Mars's orbit from raw numbers, checked it against the laws of physics, and tested whether a computer can predict it.

sections.heading: My part
sections.html:
Me: the Sun-centred analysis and the 3D animation

I wrote the whole Sun-centred orbit analysis: the Horizons data reader, the switch to a Sun-centred frame with the relative motion equation, the conservation checks and the orbital elements. I also built the 3D geocentric motion animation at the top of this page.

Team: the rest of the project

The 2D retrograde plots in the Earth-centred model, the MATLAB solver comparison and the two-body simulation, as a team of four.

blocks.title: See it for yourself
blocks.tagline: Real Horizons data, four days per frame. On the left, the view from above the Sun: Earth on the inside lane, Mars on the outside. On the right, the same moment as seen from Earth. Watch Mars's path each time Earth overtakes it.

sections.heading: What we discovered
sections.html:
24retrograde loops in our 50 years of data
60–81 dayshow long each backward drift lasts
779 daysbetween loops: the time it takes Earth to lap Mars
56–400M kmEarth–Mars distance, a more than 7× swing

Retrograde motion isn't Mars reversing. Earth is on the faster inside track, and when it overtakes Mars our line of sight swings backward against the stars for a couple of months. In the Sun-centred view nothing ever goes backward.

sections.heading: Measuring Mars's orbit from raw data (my part)
sections.text: From nothing but daily positions and velocities, I rebuilt Mars's orbit and compared it with the textbook values (Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students, Table A.1).
sections.html:
Orbital elementFrom our dataTextbook
Semi-major axis, a227.96 M km (1.524 AU)227.9 M km
Eccentricity, e0.09310.0934
Period, T687.1 days687.0 days
Inclination, i1.88°1.85°
Perihelion / aphelion206.7 / 249.2 M km–

Angular momentum and specific energy stayed constant to about 0.01% over all 50 years, exactly what a two-body orbit predicts. That check is also how I knew the whole data pipeline was right.

sections.heading: How my code works, step by step
sections.html:
1. Pull the data

    Daily position and velocity vectors from NASA JPL Horizons, 1600 to 1650. The useful part of each file sits between the $$SOE and $$EOE markers, so a small reader cuts it out and loads it into a table.

    See my Python
    block = content[start + len('$$SOE'):end]
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(block), names=columns)
  2. Move the camera to the Sun

    Horizons gives Mars and the Sun as seen from Earth. Subtracting one from the other gives Mars as seen from the Sun. That's the relative motion equation:

    rMars/Sun = rMars/Earth − rSun/Earth

    Watch out for reference frames. Horizons can measure coordinates from the plane of Earth's orbit (ecliptic) or from Earth's equator (ICRF). Those two are tilted 23.4° apart, Earth's axial tilt, so both files must use the same one. Mix them and Mars's orbit comes out tilted 21.8° instead of 1.9°.

    See my Python
    r_se = -r_sun            # Earth, seen from the Sun
r_sm = r_se + r_planet   # Mars, seen from the Sun
  3. Check the physics

    In a two-body orbit, two quantities can never change: angular momentum and specific energy. If they drift, the data or the code is wrong.

    h = r × vangular momentum
    ε = v22 − μrspecific energy

    μ is the Sun's gravitational parameter, 1.327 × 1011 km³/s².

    See my Python
    h_vec  = np.cross(r, v)
energy = 0.5*v_norm**2 - mu_sun/r_norm
  4. Back out the orbit

    Those two constants are enough to rebuild the whole ellipse: its size, shape, period and tilt.

    a = −μ2εsize
    e = √1 − h2μashape
    T = 2π√a3μperiod
    i = cos−1hzhtilt
    See my Python
    a = -mu_sun / (2*mean_energy)
e = np.sqrt(1 - h**2 / (mu_sun*a))
T = 2*np.pi*np.sqrt(a**3 / mu_sun)
i = np.degrees(np.arccos(h_z / h))
  5. Predict it (team)

    Then the reverse test: start from one day's position and velocity, integrate the equation of motion forward in MATLAB, and see how long the prediction stays on top of the real thing.

    r̈ = −μr3 rtwo-body equation of motion

sections.heading: Which solver can you trust?
sections.text: We gave nine MATLAB solvers the same starting point and compared each prediction with Horizons. All of them found Mars's period of about 688 days, but their accuracy was very different.
sections.html:
SolverAvg. error vs. Horizons, 50 yrRun time, 1,000 yr
ode890.45%5.1 s
ode23t0.53%14.6 s
ode23tb1.86%15.1 s
ode23s3.31%15.4 s
ode234.77%2.3 s
ode1135.00%3.9 s
ode786.36%29.4 s
ode15s14.38%Diverges
ode4527.67%Diverges
sections.text2:
**The surprise:** **ode45**, MATLAB's go-to solver, was the worst, with 27.7% average error, and it diverged over 1,000 years. **ode89** was about 60× more accurate. Even at a tolerance near 10⁻¹⁵ the prediction never matches Horizons perfectly, because the real Mars is also pulled by Jupiter and the other planets. That gap is the limit of the two-body model, not of the solver.

**Is that result normal?** Yes: orbits are smooth, which is where high-order methods like ode89 shine, and NASA's GMAT mission-design software uses an 8th/9th-order Runge-Kutta integrator by default. One caveat: we compared the solvers at MATLAB's default error tolerances. Tightening them would narrow the gap, especially for ode45 and ode113, at the cost of run time.

sections.heading: Where this applies
sections.html:
Mission planning
Launch windows

Mars missions launch roughly every 26 months. That's the 779-day rhythm in our data: the best time to leave depends on how Earth and Mars line up.

Communications
Talking to a rover

A radio signal takes 3 to 22 minutes to reach Mars, depending on where the planets are. Commands can't be live, so rovers need autonomy.

Verification
Testing flight software

Energy and angular momentum checks are a cheap, powerful test for any orbit simulator. If they drift, something is wrong before anything flies.

Simulation
Picking the right solver

The default isn't always the best. For long propagations, measure error and run time against real data before trusting the result.

blocks.title: Phasing Rendezvous Planner
blocks.tagline: Two spacecraft share an elliptical orbit, with the target 75° ahead. How does the chaser catch it, and how much fuel does it cost? I wrote a Python solver for this. The animation below runs the same math live.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: Chaser P sits at periapsis of orbit O₁ (a = 10,750 km, e = 0.3488). Target B is at a true anomaly of 75°. P fires a tangential burn at periapsis to enter a slightly smaller, faster phasing orbit, catches B back at periapsis, then fires an equal and opposite burn to rejoin O₁.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text:
- Convert B's true anomaly to eccentric anomaly, then mean anomaly (Kepler's equation), then time from periapsis.
- Set the timing constraint N·T<sub>phase</sub> = t<sub>B→P</sub> + (N−1)·T<sub>O₁</sub> and solve for the phasing orbit's period and semi-major axis.
- Keep the same periapsis radius, get the angular momentum, and compute Δv = (h<sub>phase</sub> − h<sub>O₁</sub>) / r<sub>p</sub>.
- Loop over N to find the fewest revolutions that keep each burn under a 0.15 km/s fuel limit.

sections.heading: The trade-off
sections.text: Spending more revolutions phasing means each orbit only needs to be slightly shorter than O₁, so the burns get smaller. The cost is time. Drag the slider to see Δv fall as N grows. For N = 1 the solver matches the hand calculation from class: a 0.172 km/s burn into a 9,947.8 km phasing orbit.

sections.heading: Also in this course
sections.text: Hohmann transfer wait times to Venus, Mars and Neptune from the synodic period (Earth to Mars from a 183° phase angle: 300.5-day wait plus 258.8-day transfer), inclination-change Δv vs. eccentricity, and Lambert's problem in MATLAB.

card.title: CanSat Finalist
card.label: CanSat World Championship · UNAM · 2025
card.summary: A can-sized satellite dropped from up to 400 m by a drone. It had to stream live data, slow itself down with a rotor, and land with a raw egg, seeds and water intact.

image.alt: The wooden CanSat prototype with its rotor blades folded open on top

page.title: CanSat Finalist
page.tagline: **Drop it from 400 m. Keep the egg alive.** A can-sized satellite, built by a team of six, that made it to the world final at UNAM.

blocks.alt: The six-person team at the CanSat world competition in front of the 'Concurso Mundial Satélites Enlatados' banner at UNAM
blocks.caption: Team Cuantificadores CUU at the world final, Ciudad Universitaria, UNAM.

sections.heading: The challenge
sections.html:
The mission: Akai-Sakura
Plant a forest on Mars.

The competition's story: it's 2051 and a satellite has to deliver seeds and water to Utopia Planitia so trees can grow on Mars. Our job was to build the satellite and prove it works on Earth: dropped from the sky, slowed down with no motor, and landed with its cargo intact.

300–400 mrelease height, lifted by a drone
< 18 m/slanding speed, with no motor, only a rotor
< 700 gtotal mass, including an egg, seeds and 125 ml of water
$600maximum budget for the whole satellite

sections.heading: My part
sections.html:
Me: structure and shock absorption

I worked on the wooden structure, the body that holds everything inside the 2U envelope and the 700 g limit, and on the shock-absorption system that keeps the egg alive: the spring-cushioned base, plus the cushioning wrapped around the egg, which we chose by drop-testing different materials.

Team: everything else

The rotor, the flight electronics and telemetry, and the ground station, as a team of six.

sections.heading: How a flight works
sections.html:
1. 1 · LiftDrone climb

    A drone carries the CanSat up to 300–400 m.

  2. 2 · ReleaseFree fall

    Dropped. Live data streams to our ground station.

  3. 3 · 200 mRotor opens

    Blades unfold and spin like a maple seed.

  4. 4 · DescentSlow and steer

    Under 18 m/s, aiming for a 3 m bullseye.

  5. 5 · LandingCargo check

    Egg, seeds and water intact. Keep transmitting 30 s.

sections.heading: The rules that made it hard
sections.html:
The crew
A raw egg

A 60 g chicken egg rides inside as the "astronaut". It has to come back uncracked.

The cargo
Seeds and water

Native seeds and 125 ml of water in a sealed container. Not a drop can spill.

The body
Made of wood

A 2U CubeSat-sized structure, and the rules say it has to be wood.

The data
Live telemetry

Pressure, temperature, speed, acceleration and CO₂, from lift-off until 30 s after landing.

sections.heading: Our design (structure and landing: my part)
sections.text: A laser-cut wooden body sized like a 2U CubeSat, with a cradle for the egg and a sealed water container inside. Underneath, a **spring-cushioned shock-absorption base** takes the hit at landing, so the egg doesn't. On top, a **folding autogyro rotor**: no motor, the blades open at 200 m and the air spins them, like a maple seed.

figures.alt: CAD section of the wooden CanSat showing the egg cradle, internal compartments and measurements
figures.caption: CAD section: the egg's place in the middle, payload bays around it

figures.alt: The built wooden CanSat with its two rotor blades folded open on top and springs at the base
figures.caption: The real thing: blades open, springs at the base

sections.heading: Protecting the egg (my part)
sections.text: The landing is the most dangerous moment for the egg. The spring base takes the first hit, but the egg also needed its own **cushioning wrap**, light enough for the 700 g limit and small enough to fit inside the body. Instead of guessing, we tested it.
sections.html:
1. 1Pick candidates

    Several light cushioning materials that could wrap a 60 g egg.

  2. 2Wrap the egg

    Each material wrapped the same way, so the tests were fair.

  3. 3Drop it

    Repeated drop tests to see which one absorbed the most shock.

  4. 4Pick the winner

    The best absorber went into the flight CanSat.

Two layers of protection: the spring base slows the whole satellite at impact, and the wrap spreads what's left around the egg's shell instead of letting it hit one point.

sections.heading: The rotor
sections.text: The rotor is what slows the CanSat from free fall to a safe landing. We designed the hub and gave the blades a curved, wing-like profile so they **generate lift as they spin**.

figures.alt: CAD model of the rotor hub with hinged blades hanging down in the folded position
figures.caption: Rotor hub with the blades folded

figures.alt: CAD model of a single curved rotor blade

sections.heading: The electronics
sections.text: Our own flight board, with the team name printed on it, reads the sensors and streams the data live to the ground station. Everything, antenna included, had to fit inside the wooden body and run on **9 V batteries only**.

page.title: Ultrasonic Thickness and Flaw Testing
page.tagline: **Seeing inside metal with sound.** Hands-on ultrasonic testing training at NMSU's Non-Destructive Evaluation Lab.

blocks.alt: Sonatest flaw detector showing an A-scan with echo peaks, connected to a straight probe pressed on a steel block
blocks.caption: My setup in the training: a straight probe on a steel block, and its echoes on the flaw detector.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: A probe sends a short burst of **high-frequency sound** into the metal, far above what we can hear. The sound bounces off whatever it meets: the back wall of the part, or a crack, void or corroded spot hiding inside. The flaw detector plots those echoes as peaks on an **A-scan**.
sections.html:
d = v · t2depth or thickness

The echo's timing tells you where things are. Sound travels through steel at about 5.9 km/s. Measure how long the echo takes to come back, multiply by the speed and halve it (down and back), and you get the plate's thickness, or exactly how deep a hidden flaw sits.

sections.heading: The training
sections.text: I completed the **Certification to Degree (C2D) Ultrasonic Testing training** at NMSU's NDE Lab. It's part of a Department of Defense-funded consortium between Arizona State University, NMSU and Navajo Technical University that builds pathways into advanced manufacturing and non-destructive evaluation.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html:
Aerospace
Cracks you can't see

Aircraft parts are checked for hidden fatigue cracks without cutting them open or taking them out of service.

Industry
Corrosion and thickness

Pipes, tanks and pressure vessels are scanned for wall thinning long before they leak.

Manufacturing
Welds and printed parts

Ultrasound finds voids and lack of fusion in welds and 3D-printed metal before they ever reach service.

Safety
Test without breaking

The part you inspect is the part that flies or ships. Nothing gets destroyed to prove it's good.

page.title: Scratch-Built RC Plane
page.tagline: **Our first airplane. Six seconds of flight.** A freshman Statics project that became my first lesson in how aircraft stay balanced.

blocks.alt: Small hand-built model plane on a street at dusk, with a craft-stick frame, an orange propeller on an electric motor and a toy pilot
blocks.caption: Our scratch-built plane: craft-stick frame, electric motor up front, and a very small pilot.

sections.heading: The project
sections.text: This was our very first project, in freshman-year **Statics**. At that point we were still far from understanding how planes really behave in the air, but that was the point: we used this build to start learning about flight.

sections.heading: Where statics comes in
sections.text:
Our work was all about **where things go**. We worked out how to arrange the components (motor, battery and electronics) and studied how commercial aircraft arrange the weight of their different components so the whole plane balances.

The key idea is simple: the plane's **center of gravity** has to sit at the right spot relative to where the wing produces **lift**. Too far back and the nose pitches up; too far forward and it dives.

blocks.title: Balance it, then fly it
blocks.tagline: Slide the battery until the center of gravity lines up with the lift. Then it's time to fly.

sections.heading: How it went
sections.html:
≈ 6 sof flight before it crashed
Year 1our first hands-on look at flight

Short flight, big lesson. It flew for about six seconds before it crashed, but we learned a lot, and it's where my interest in how aircraft fly really started.

sections.heading: What I'd change now, and what I learned
sections.html:
Balance
Center of gravity

Put the CG about 25–30% of the way back along the wing, a little ahead of where the lift acts, so the plane naturally settles nose-down instead of sitting on a knife edge.

Lift
Wing size

Size the wing from the plane's weight (wing loading) instead of by eye, so it makes enough lift at a speed we can actually launch it at.

Control
Tail and control surfaces

A bigger horizontal tail for pitch stability, plus an elevator and rudder sized to correct the flight, not just hope it stays level.

Testing
Test before it flies

Hand-glide tests and a balance check first, then powered flight, changing one thing at a time so we'd know what fixed what.

Lessons learned: balance is only the start. A plane also has to be stable (it recovers on its own) and controllable (you can correct it). Six seconds of flight taught us to design for both, and to test small before testing big.
